 1    I. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF THE CASE

2    COMES NOW John B. Bradley III ("Intervenor"), appearing pro se, owner and steward of the
3    Lazy S Ranch in Bell County, Texas, and ﬁles this Initial Brief in opposition to the Application
4    of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation
5    ("Applicants") for a Certiﬁcate of Convenience and Necessity ("CCN") associated with the
6    Bell County East–Big Hill 765-kV Transmission Line Project.

 7   Intervenor owns and manages the Lazy S Ranch, a historic working ranch that has
 8   remained under continuous ownership and stewardship by the Bradley family for
 9   approximately one hundred years. The property represents ﬁve generations of agricultural,
10   ranching, conservation, and family stewardship. It contains historic ranch structures,
11   cemetery resources, a spring-fed artesian well system, active cattle operations, wildlife
12   habitat, hunting operations, and the future homesite intended for Intervenor and his family
13   following retirement from more than twenty-three years of military service.

14   Intervenor's testimony was admitted pursuant to Texas Rules of Evidence 602 and 701 and
15   was based upon personal knowledge, ﬁrsthand observations, family stewardship of the
16   property, and direct experience managing the ranch and its resources. The testimony
17   addressed impacts to community values, historical and aesthetic values, environmental
18   integrity, agricultural operations, wildlife habitat, water resources, and future residential
19   use.

20   The evidence demonstrates that Applicants failed to establish by a preponderance of the
21   evidence that routing Segments E8, E9, F21, F22, and G71 through the Lazy S Ranch
22   satisﬁes the requirements of PURA §§ 37.051 and 37.056(c), 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101,
23   or the public convenience and necessity standard.

24   The evidence further demonstrates that the proposed route would impose substantial and
25   permanent burdens upon a historically signiﬁcant ranch property while providing only
26   generalized and largely regional beneﬁts that Applicants failed to quantify or adequately
27   support through project-speciﬁc evidence.

28   Accordingly, the Application should be denied. In the alternative, the Commission should
29   reject Segments E8, E9, F21, F22, and G71 and select a route that avoids the Lazy S Ranch
30   and better satisﬁes the statutory requirements governing route selection and public
31   convenience and necessity.

32   II. APPLICABLE LAW AND BURDEN OF PROOF


                                                                     INITIAL BRIEF OF JOHN B. BRADLEY
                                                                                 PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
                                                                       SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349
                                                                                        Page 2 of 28
 1    Applicants bear the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that the
2    requested Certiﬁcate of Convenience and Necessity satisﬁes the requirements of PURA
3    and applicable Commission rules.

4    PURA §37.056(c) requires the Commission to consider:

5       1. The adequacy of existing service;

6       2. The need for additional service;

7       3. The e ect of granting the certiﬁcate on the recipient and any electric utility serving
8          the proximate area;

9       4. Community values;

10      5. Recreational and park areas;

11      6. Historical and aesthetic values;

12      7. Environmental integrity; and

13      8. The probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers.

14   Additionally, 16 Tex. Admin. Code §25.101(b)(3)(B) requires consideration of routing that
15   reasonably minimizes adverse impacts on landowners and communities and, where
16   practicable, utilizes compatible existing rights-of-way and corridors.

17   The Commission must further evaluate whether the proposed route serves the public
18   convenience and necessity and whether the asserted public beneﬁts outweigh the burdens
19   imposed upon a ected landowners.

20   The burden does not shift to a ected landowners to prove that the route is improper.
21   Rather, Applicants must a irmatively demonstrate that the selected route represents the
22   most reasonable balance between the project's asserted public beneﬁts and the resulting
23   impacts to private property, historical resources, environmental resources, agricultural
24   operations, and community values.

25   Where signiﬁcant uncertainty remains regarding environmental impacts, historical
26   resources, archaeological resources, routing impacts, or consumer beneﬁts, Applicants
27   have failed to satisfy their burden.

28   The record demonstrates that such uncertainty remains throughout this proceeding.

 1    Accordingly, the Commission should conclude that Applicants failed to establish by a
2    preponderance of the evidence that the proposed route satisﬁes the requirements of PURA
3    §37.056(c), 16 Tex. Admin. Code §25.101, and the public convenience and necessity
4    standard.

5    III. APPLICANTS FAILED TO ESTABLISH NEED, PUBLIC BENEFIT, OR PUBLIC
6    CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY

 7   The central question before the Commission is not whether ERCOT has identiﬁed projected
 8   future transmission needs somewhere within Texas. The question is whether Applicants
 9   established by a preponderance of the evidence that the Bell County East–Big Hill 765-kV
10   Transmission Line Project, and speciﬁcally the routing a ecting Segments E8, E9, F21, F22,
11   and G71, satisﬁes the requirements of PURA §37.056(c), 16 Tex. Admin. Code §25.101, and
12   the public convenience and necessity standard.

13   The evidence demonstrates that Applicants failed to meet that burden.

14   Applicants rely heavily upon projected future load growth, future generation development,
15   import capability, House Bill 5066, ERCOT planning assumptions, and the Permian Basin
16   Reliability Plan. However, reliance upon regional planning assumptions does not constitute
17   proof that the speciﬁc route selected through the Lazy S Ranch is necessary or represents
18   the route that best satisﬁes the statutory requirements imposed by PURA §37.056(c).

19   The record reﬂects that Applicants largely relied upon ERCOT planning conclusions rather
20   than presenting independent project-speciﬁc evidence demonstrating that this particular
21   transmission line is required to maintain reliability or improve service within Bell County or
22   the communities directly a ected by the proposed route.

23   While Intervenor does not dispute that ERCOT, the Legislature, and the Commission have
24   identiﬁed projected future transmission needs associated with growth in West Texas, the
25   existence of a regional transmission objective does not relieve Applicants of their burden to
26   demonstrate that the selected route appropriately balances reliability objectives against
27   impacts to landowners, community values, historical resources, environmental integrity,
28   agricultural operations, and the public interest.

29   PURA §37.056(c) requires more than proof that additional transmission infrastructure may
30   be beneﬁcial. The statute requires the Commission to evaluate whether the proposed route
31   serves the public convenience and necessity when all statutory factors are considered
32   together.


                                                                    INITIAL BRIEF OF JOHN B. BRADLEY
                                                                                PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
                                                                      SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349

 1    Applicants repeatedly asserted reliability beneﬁts, increased transfer capability, and
2    support for future generation development. Yet Applicants presented little evidence
3    demonstrating that this project will lower residential electric bills, reduce transmission
4    costs, improve a ordability for Texas families, or provide measurable economic beneﬁts to
5    ordinary consumers.

 6   Applicant witness Corin Cooley acknowledged that signiﬁcant project cost assumptions
 7   were developed during the fall of 2025 and ﬁnalized in March 2026. 1 Despite the magnitude
 8   of the proposed investment, Applicants failed to quantify any direct reduction in consumer
 9   electric costs attributable to this project. 2 Accordingly, Applicants failed to establish the
10   "probable improvement of service or lowering of cost to consumers" required by PURA
11   §37.056(c).

12   The evidentiary record also revealed signiﬁcant deﬁciencies regarding environmental
13   review and routing analysis.

14   Commission Sta witness John Poole acknowledged that he did not independently verify
15   all environmental conclusions contained within the environmental assessment. 3 Mr. Poole
16   further acknowledged that he did not independently review ﬂoodplain studies and did not
17   evaluate documented July 2025 ﬂood impacts a ecting Route 487.4 These admissions
18   demonstrate that important environmental assumptions underlying the routing analysis
19   were not independently veriﬁed.

20   Mr. Poole acknowledged that cultural features are a factor that should be considered
21   during transmission-line routing, yet testiﬁed that he was unaware of any proposed route
22   that paralleled cultural features and further acknowledged that he did not speciﬁcally
23   recommend consultation with the Comanche Nation regarding cultural resources. 5

24   Likewise, Applicants' environmental witness Matt Marusak acknowledged that the
25   Environmental Assessment identiﬁed a "high potential for encountering additional eligible
26   or landmark caliber resources," admitted that additional unidentiﬁed cultural resources
27   may exist within the study area, and conceded that he could not state that all culturally
28   signiﬁcant resources had been identiﬁed.6 Mr. Marusak further acknowledged that he had
29   not personally walked portions of the a ected corridor and had not consulted landowners

10   impactful alternatives utilizing existing compatible corridors to the maximum extent
11   practicable.

12   The Commission's duty is not merely to determine whether transmission infrastructure is
13   needed somewhere within Texas. The Commission must determine whether the speciﬁc
14   route selected appropriately balances public beneﬁts against private burdens.

15   The evidence demonstrates that Applicants ask the Commission to impose permanent
16   burdens upon private property owners in exchange for generalized and largely regional
17   beneﬁts. Those beneﬁts remain speculative and di icult to quantify. By contrast, the
18   burdens imposed upon a ected landowners are immediate, direct, certain, and
19   permanent.

20   Accordingly, Applicants failed to establish by a preponderance of the evidence that:

21   (a) the selected route is necessary beyond generalized ERCOT planning assumptions;

22   (b) the project will lower costs or improve a ordability for Texas consumers;

23   (c) the project's beneﬁts outweigh the burdens imposed upon a ected landowners;

24   (d) environmental impacts have been adequately evaluated;

25   (e) historical and cultural resources have been adequately considered; and

26   (f) the proposed route satisﬁes the public convenience and necessity requirements of
27   PURA §37.056(c).

3    IV. COMMUNITY VALUES, CONTINUOUS FAMILY STEWARDSHIP, AND PRIVATE
4    PROPERTY IMPACTS

5    PURA §37.056(c) expressly requires the Commission to consider community values when
6    evaluating a proposed transmission route.

 7   The evidence demonstrates that the Lazy S Ranch represents far more than an individual
 8   tract of private property. It is a century-old working ranch that has remained under
 9   continuous ownership and stewardship by the same family for approximately one hundred
10   years. The ranch reﬂects ﬁve generations of agricultural use, conservation stewardship,
11   ranch management, and family investment. 9

12   Unlike speculative development property, the Lazy S Ranch remains an active and
13   productive part of the Bell County community. The property continues to support cattle
14   operations, wildlife management activities, hunting operations, conservation e orts, and
15   long-term family use. The ranch remains part of the agricultural and rural character that
16   deﬁnes this portion of Bell County.10

17   The historical continuity of ownership is particularly signiﬁcant. Few properties in Central
18   Texas remain substantially intact after approximately one hundred years of continuous
19   family stewardship. The ranch has been preserved through multiple generations despite
20   changing economic conditions, urban expansion, and development pressures. The
21   continued stewardship of the property reﬂects a long-term commitment to responsible
22   land management and preservation of the ranch's agricultural, environmental, and
23   historical resources.11

24   Based upon my personal knowledge and observations, the proposed route directly
25   threatens that continuity.

26   Following more than twenty-three years of service as an Army o icer, including multiple
27   deployments and assignments around the world, my family and I intend to return
28   permanently to Bell County and establish our future residence on the Lazy S Ranch. The

7    A. The Lazy S Ranch Constitutes an Intact Historic Ranch Landscape

8    The historical signiﬁcance of the Lazy S Ranch extends far beyond the existence of
9    individual structures.

10   Based upon my personal knowledge, family records, observations, and continuous
11   stewardship of the property, the ranch has remained under substantially continuous family
12   ownership and stewardship for approximately one hundred years. The property represents
13   ﬁve generations of ranching, agricultural use, conservation stewardship, and family
14   occupation.

15   The ranch contains a historic ranch house, ranch-hand cabin, barns, agricultural
16   structures, historic water improvements, cemetery resources, and supporting ranch
17   infrastructure dating to the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. These resources
18   remain interconnected within a functioning historic ranch landscape that continues to
19   serve the same agricultural and stewardship purposes for which they were originally
20   established.15

21   The signiﬁcance of these resources derives not only from their age, but from their
22   continued relationship to one another and their contribution to a largely intact historic
23   setting. Collectively, they tell the story of settlement, ranching, agriculture, and family
24   stewardship in Bell County and Central Texas over multiple generations.

25   Unlike isolated historic structures that may be relocated or restored, a historic ranch
26   landscape derives much of its signiﬁcance from its setting, viewshed, spatial relationships,
27   and continuity of use. Once fragmented by a major transmission corridor, that historic
28   context cannot be fully restored.

29   The proposed transmission corridor would introduce steel lattice structures approaching

4    B. Historical Stewardship Warrants Signiﬁcant Weight Under PURA §37.056(c)

5    The Commission should give substantial weight to the unusual continuity of ownership and
6    stewardship associated with the Lazy S Ranch.

7    Many properties a ected by transmission projects have experienced subdivision,
8    development, or frequent ownership changes over time. By contrast, the Lazy S Ranch has
9    remained under the stewardship of the same family for approximately one century.

10   The preservation of the property through ﬁve generations reﬂects a long-term commitment
11   to responsible stewardship of agricultural resources, water resources, wildlife habitat, and
12   historical improvements. Such continuity is increasingly rare and constitutes an important
13   historical value that should be considered by the Commission.

14   The proposed route threatens not merely individual improvements, but the continued
15   preservation of a historically signiﬁcant family ranch that has remained intact through
16   multiple generations.

19   improvements.

21   contains perennial spring-fed water resources, artesian water, riparian corridors, elevated
22   terrain, wildlife resources, and natural features historically associated with long-term
23   human habitation and settlement.17

24   The ranch exists within the broader archaeological landscape of Central Texas and is
25   located in proximity to the internationally recognized Gault Site, one of the most signiﬁcant
26   archaeological discoveries in North America.18

7    VI. ENVIRONMENTAL INTEGRITY AND WATER RESOURCES

8    PURA §37.056(c) requires the Commission to consider environmental integrity when
